Front: What loop do agentic applications run?
Back: They run an observe-reason-act-observe loop: the model sees current context, chooses a tool or response, incorporates results, and continues until the task is done or blocked.

Front: Which agentic pattern fits a fixed three-stage code review (style, then security, then documentation)?
Back: Prompt chaining, because the steps are known and fixed; chaining adds reliability by constraining the model to a known sequence.

Front: Which pattern fits routing invoices, receipts, and contracts to different extraction tools?
Back: Routing: inputs fall into distinct handling categories, so you classify then dispatch to the right handler.

Front: Which pattern fits debugging an intermittent backend failure where each finding changes the plan?
Back: Dynamic decomposition, because the next step genuinely depends on what the model just learned; a fixed checklist would miss the actual cause.

Front: Which pattern fits a research coordinator that decides which specialist subagents to invoke?
Back: Orchestrator-workers: a coordinator chooses and delegates subtasks rather than following a fixed chain.

Front: When should you avoid the parallel-subagents pattern?
Back: When workstreams depend on each other's results, when the partition would split a logical unit, or when sequential streaming output matters more than throughput.

Front: A billing-dispute workflow always runs verify identity, fetch invoice, check policy, propose adjustment. Chaining or dynamic decomposition?
Back: Prompt chaining: the steps are genuinely fixed, so chaining gives reliability and consistent outputs; dynamic decomposition would invite unnecessary tool calls.

Front: A security incident triage must decide whether to pull logs, query a SIEM, page on-call, or all three. Which pattern?
Back: Dynamic decomposition: the next move only becomes clear after the current finding, so a fixed chain would produce shallow analyses.

Front: Why is the choice of agentic pattern framed as matching the shape of work rather than picking the best pattern?
Back: Each pattern trades reliability against adaptability; chaining suits fixed steps while decomposition suits exploratory work, so the right one depends on the task structure.

Front: The user asks the coordinator to summarize three sentences it just retrieved. Delegate to a subagent or answer directly?
Back: Answer directly: delegation adds a tool call, fresh context, separate invocation, and result passing; that overhead is wasteful when the coordinator already has the context and the work is small.

Front: Name three cases where delegating to a subagent is worthwhile despite its overhead.
Back: When the task would flood the coordinator's context, when it needs a different prompt or tool set (specialist persona), or when it can run in parallel with other work.

Front: What is the partition-then-parallel pattern for auditing 50 repositories?
Back: The coordinator divides the input into N roughly equal chunks, spawns N subagents (one per chunk), and synthesizes their uniform structured outputs.

Front: In partition-then-parallel work, why balance partitions by expected effort, not raw count?
Back: Total elapsed time becomes max(subagent_durations); if a few partitions are far heavier, the slowest one dictates total time and the parallelism is wasted.

Front: Does a subagent automatically share the parent agent's conversation state?
Back: No. A subagent starts a fresh conversation and sees only what the parent explicitly passes plus its own AgentDefinition; it does not see prior user turns, assistant turns, or tool results.

Front: Since subagents do not inherit context, what must the parent put in the subagent prompt?
Back: Everything the subagent needs: the goal, relevant findings, constraints, source references, and the expected output shape.

Front: Why doesn't a "resume the previous research subagent" pattern exist by default?
Back: Calling the Agent/Task tool again starts a brand-new agent; for continuity the parent must persist an identifier or include the prior summary in the new prompt.

Front: Critique the subagent handoff "Synthesize the findings."
Back: It is too vague; a good handoff specifies the records, requires preserving uncertainty, citing each claim with its source_id, and separating established from contested findings.

Front: For final report generation requiring citations, what should the coordinator pass to the report subagent?
Back: A structured source index mapping claims to source IDs, URLs, excerpts, dates, and confidence/uncertainty notes - not only a prose summary.

Front: Why shouldn't every subagent inherit every tool?
Back: More tools increase selection complexity and can lead agents outside their role; restricting tools to what each subagent needs improves focus and security.

Front: What tools does a synthesis subagent that should only work from supplied findings need?
Back: Generally no external search tools; it should work only from the findings the coordinator passes so it does not introduce unsourced content.

Front: In the Claude Agent SDK, what must be in the parent's allowedTools for it to spawn subagents?
Back: The delegation tool itself (typically named Task or Agent); without it the parent has no callable interface to launch the subagent definitions.

Front: An orchestrator describes delegation but no subagent ever runs. What is the most likely cause?
Back: The Task/Agent tool is not in the parent's allowedTools, so the parent has no interface to launch subagents even though the definitions exist.

Front: When should a coordinator start independent tasks concurrently?
Back: When the tasks do not depend on each other's output; parallel execution turns elapsed time into max(durations) instead of sum, especially for I/O-bound work.

Front: When must you NOT parallelize two tasks?
Back: When the second task needs the first task's output - e.g., document analysis cannot inspect sources until the sources are identified.

Front: Describe the common three-phase agentic phasing pattern.
Back: Serial decomposition (one call plans the independent units), then parallel execution (each unit runs concurrently), then serial synthesis (one final call assembles results).

Front: For which kind of subtasks does the parallel phase win the most latency back?
Back: I/O-bound subtasks (fetches, searches, document analyses), because elapsed time becomes max(durations); CPU- or token-bound work sees a smaller speedup.

Front: Why persist structured exports rather than only transcripts for long multi-agent workflows?
Back: On resume the coordinator can load a manifest and inject only relevant state into each agent prompt, which is more efficient than replaying every subagent transcript.

Front: What does a workflow state manifest typically contain?
Back: Workflow id, completed steps, per-document status with claim IDs, and open gaps - durable structured state, not raw conversation.

Front: Why must research agents preserve publication or data-collection dates with each claim?
Back: Without dates a synthesis agent may treat older and newer statistics as contradictory when they actually show a trend over time.

Front: What should research subagents output per finding for trustworthy synthesis?
Back: Claim, source ID and location, publication/data date, methodology notes, source confidence language, and whether the finding is established, contested, or insufficiently supported.

Front: When should a customer-service agent escalate to a human?
Back: When the user explicitly asks and the issue cannot be resolved without overriding them, the issue needs authority the agent lacks, a policy exception or high-value transaction is involved, no meaningful progress is possible, or tool results show an unsafe state needing human judgment.

Front: Why is "escalate after three failed tool calls" a poor escalation rule?
Back: The category and impact of a failure matter more than the count; a simplistic counter ignores whether the failure is recoverable or critical.

Front: What should an escalation handoff contain?
Back: A structured handoff: customer ID, issue type, root cause, relevant records, amount, actions taken, and recommended next action - not just the first complaint or a raw transcript dump.

Front: A frustrated user asks for a human but the issue is straightforward and resolvable. What should the agent do?
Back: Acknowledge the frustration, offer the immediate resolution while preserving their choice to be transferred, and let them pick - do not silently perform the account action.

Front: Which customer-service rules must be enforced programmatically rather than by prompt?
Back: Hard rules: refunds above a threshold, reimbursements needing manager approval, regulated financial/healthcare workflows, and destructive infrastructure operations.

Front: Why put a reimbursement threshold rule inside the process_reimbursement tool itself?
Back: So the model cannot bypass it by choosing the wrong tool or setting an approval flag incorrectly; the tool disburses below the threshold and creates a pending approval above it.

Front: Where should a credit-limit threshold value come from, and why?
Back: From a server-controlled source (feature flag, policy service, account record), not a model-passed parameter, so the model cannot raise the cap by setting something like override=true.

Front: Describe preview-then-execute with single-use tokens for a high-impact action.
Back: A preview tool returns a redacted summary plus a short-lived one-time token bound to that payload; the user confirms; the execute tool consumes the token. The model cannot forge or reuse a token with different parameters.

Front: Why re-verify the caller's authority on every tool invocation even when the model behaved correctly?
Back: Tools live inside the trust boundary and must validate; "the model already checked policy" is not a defense against adversarial input or prompt injection.

Front: What does defense-in-depth mean for customer-service compliance?
Back: Prompt rules bias the agent, tool implementations enforce the hard rule, and audit logs detect violations - prose rules alone can be pushed past by adversarial users or prompt injection.

Front: How should an agent handle a tool failing mid-workflow (graceful degradation)?
Back: Explain what was verified, state what could not be completed, be transparent about the system issue, and offer next steps like retry, escalation, or notification.

Front: Why prefer "here is what is done, here is what is pending" over a flat success message after partial completion?
Back: Users tolerate visible incompleteness but not later discovering a supposedly completed action silently rolled back; never claim a side effect that did not finish.

Front: When the same tool keeps failing on the same input, what should the agent do?
Back: Treat it as a signal to switch strategies - try a different tool, ask a clarifying question, or escalate - rather than burning more retries on the same call.

Front: Why not use a full research pipeline for a simple factual query?
Back: The coordinator should choose a smaller path for simple queries; running the whole pipeline wastes calls and latency for facts that need no decomposition.

Front: If one-pass research finds gaps, what should the coordinator do?
Back: Trigger a targeted follow-up search; a strict single-pass design leaves known gaps unanswered.

Front: Why not pass raw 100K-token outputs between every agent in a pipeline?
Back: It floods context and cost; pass structured summaries plus source indexes so downstream agents get what they need without the bulk.

Front: When should you give subagents goals and quality criteria instead of brittle step-by-step search strings?
Back: When adaptability matters; over-prescribed steps stop the subagent from adjusting to what it finds, while goals plus criteria let it adapt.

Front: What is the trade-off of dynamic decomposition versus a fixed chain?
Back: Dynamic plans adapt to findings but are unpredictable and hard to budget, so you must set explicit termination criteria and step caps.

Front: Why is starting a fixed debugging checklist often the wrong approach for an intermittent failure?
Back: A pre-written checklist often misses the actual cause and runs every step regardless; the cause only becomes clear after each finding, which is what dynamic decomposition handles.

Front: For multi-issue customer sessions across many turns, how can the agent reliably answer "what happened with my refund?"
Back: Track each issue's current status (order ID, amounts, resolution state) in structured state independent of the linear conversation.
